extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers/importers/distributors, hazard classifiers, label preparers, SDS authors, safety professionals, and OSHA stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for classifying chemicals and communicating hazards under the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) as updated to align primarily with GHS Rev. 7. Covers definitions, classification categories, testing/standards, labeling flexibilities, and corrections to prior HCS provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive toxicity definition and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproductive toxicity refers to adverse effects on sexual function and fertility in adult males and females, as well as developmental toxicity in the offspring, occurring after exposure to a substance or mixture. Some reproductive toxic effects cannot be clearly assigned to either impairment of sexual function and fertility or to developmental toxicity. Nonetheless, substances and mixtures with these effects shall be classified as reproductive toxicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a substance or mixture produces adverse effects on sexual function/fertility or developmental toxicity in offspring it must be classified as a reproductive toxicant even when effects cannot be cleanly assigned to one subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific target organ toxicity—single exposure (STOT-SE)
rubrics_metrics.description: STOT-SE refers to specific, non-lethal toxic effects on target organs occurring after a single exposure to a substance or mixture. All significant health effects that can impair function, both reversible and irreversible, immediate and/or delayed and not specifically addressed in A.1 to A.7 and A.10 are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify single-exposure organ effects under STOT-SE; do not include effects that are addressed in A.1–A.7 or A.10. Specific target organ toxicity following repeated exposure is classified under STOT-RE and is therefore excluded here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific target organ toxicity—repeated exposure (STOT-RE)
rubrics_metrics.description: STOT-RE refers to specific toxic effects on target organs occurring after repeated exposure to a substance or mixture. All significant health effects that can impair function, both reversible and irreversible, immediate and/or delayed and not specifically addressed in A.1 to A.7 and A.10 are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify repeated-exposure organ effects under STOT-RE; single-event exposures should be classified under STOT-SE instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration hazard and aspiration definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiration hazard refers to severe acute effects such as chemical pneumonia, pulmonary injury or death occurring after aspiration of a substance or mixture. Aspiration means the entry of a liquid or solid chemical directly through the oral or nasal cavity, or indirectly from vomiting, into the trachea and lower respiratory system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substances likely to be aspirated causing severe pulmonary effects must be classified as aspiration hazards and labeled/communicated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency: replace 'toxicity category' with 'hazard category'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2012 HCS used 'hazard category' and 'toxicity category' inconsistently; OSHA proposed to delete the term 'toxicity category' and replace it with 'hazard category' throughout Appendix A (paragraphs A.0.5, A.1, A.3, A.8, A.9, and A.10) to ensure appropriate and consistent usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'hazard category' consistently in regulatory text and guidance to align with Rev. 7 and remove potential ambiguity caused by interchangeable usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory language: change 'should' to 'must/shall' where required
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed to update provisions to make clear they are mandatory; for example, change the term 'should' to 'must' in paragraph A.3.4.3.3 (now A.3.3.3.3) to clarify that the cut-off value/concentrations in Table A.3.3 are mandatory when determining if a mixture must be classified as seriously damaging to the eye or an eye irritant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where GHS guidance is adopted into the HCS, the agency will change non-mandatory wording to mandatory ('should' → 'shall'/'must') in specified places so specified threshold values and procedures are required for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles corrections: include Appendix A.4 for sensitization
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA erroneously omitted Appendix A.4 (respiratory or skin sensitization) from the list of health hazards referenced in the 'concentration of mixtures' paragraph at A.0.5.1.3 and from the 'interpolation within one toxicity category' paragraph at A.0.5.1.4; OSHA proposed to add a reference to Appendix A.4 to clarify the concentration of mixtures bridging principle and interpolation bridging principle apply to respiratory and skin sensitization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers must apply the concentration-of-mixtures bridging principle and interpolation within one toxicity category to respiratory and skin sensitization hazards per the corrected references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add desensitized explosives hazard class and related categories in Appendix B
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed adding a new hazard class (desensitized explosives) and additional hazard categories (splitting Category 1 into 1A and 1B and further subdividing Category 1A into flammable gases, chemically unstable gases and pyrophoric gases in the Flammable Gases class, as well as nonflammable aerosols in the Aerosols class) to align with GHS Rev. 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt new classes/categories to improve differentiation and communication of physical hazards; classifiers should consult the updated Appendix B and accompanying notes for how to identify desensitized explosives and the new categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update references to consensus standards and test methods (Rev.7) but do not require retesting of previously-classified chemicals
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed to update consensus standards and testing methods referenced in Appendix B in accordance with Rev. 7 to ensure data considered for classification incorporate updated scientific principles, but clarified this is not implying data from older methods are invalid nor that classifiers must retest or reclassify chemicals due to updated methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use updated standards and methods for new classifications; previously classified chemicals need not be automatically reevaluated solely because referenced methods have changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division 1.6 explosives classification wording: 'only' → 'predominantly'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rev. 3, one criterion for classifying an article as Division 1.6 explosive was that it contains 'only' extremely insensitive detonating chemicals; Rev. 7 states criteria are met if the article 'predominantly' contains extremely insensitive detonating chemicals. OSHA proposed changing 'only' to 'predominantly' in B.1.2(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt 'predominantly' language to align with UN Manual of Tests and Criteria and reduce classification confusion for manufacturers/importers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes for desensitized explosives (Note 2 and Note 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Note 2: explosives for which explosive properties have been suppressed or reduced by being wetted with water or alcohols, diluted with other substances, or dissolved/suspended in water or other liquid substances must be classified as desensitized explosives. Proposed Note 3: some chemicals exempt from classification as explosives under UN TDG guidelines still have explosive properties, which must be communicated in Section 2 (Hazard identification) and Section 9 (Physical and chemical properties) of the SDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate the notes as requirements in the HCS (change 'may be a candidate for classification as' to 'shall be classified as') and revise GHS terminology to HCS-appropriate vocabulary (e.g., 'chemicals' vs 'substances and mixtures').

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification on desensitization by mixing with solids
rubrics_metrics.description: DOD suggested adding reference to desensitizing by mixing with inert solids (e.g., silica); OSHA declined, stating the note's purpose is to alert classifiers a mixture may be a desensitized explosive and is not intended to list every mechanism. OSHA noted mixing with solids is not excluded by 'diluted with other substances' but that adding solids does not unequivocally abate explosive hazard and may require reevaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers should not assume solids always desensitize explosives; any mixture possibly altering explosive properties should be evaluated case-by-case and may require reclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling flexibility: use of Rev.9 labeling elements case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA indicated that although it is not adopting Rev. 9 wholesale, a label preparer may, on a case-by-case basis, determine that using label elements prescribed in Rev. 9 for explosives would be in compliance with the HCS if the label preparer can show the Rev. 9 elements are more appropriate and therefore in full compliance with the HCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label preparers may use alternative label elements (signal word, hazard statement, pictogram) from later GHS revisions when justified by analysis of the explosive, leveraging HCS flexibilities (Appendix C notes and C.2.x flexibilities). Such deviations must demonstrate compliance with HCS requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of Flammable Gases Category 1 into 1A and 1B
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed subdividing Category 1 for flammable gases into two subcategories, 1A and 1B, and specifying that pyrophoric gases and chemically unstable gases are to be classified as Category 1A, aligning with Rev. 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subdivision provides downstream users better understanding of severity (flammability limit, burning velocity) and supports selection of less flammable alternatives; these subdivisions do not change transportation classification where both remain Category 1 for transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrophoric gas definition alignment and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously defined as 'a chemical in a gaseous state that will ignite spontaneously in air at a temperature of 130°F (54.4°C) or below.' GHS defines as 'a flammable gas that is liable to ignite spontaneously in air at a temperature of 54°C [130°F] or below.' OSHA proposed aligning with 'liable to ignite' wording and moving the pyrophoric gas definition into Appendix B.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt 'liable to ignite' wording to be technically accurate (allows for delayed ignition); OSHA anticipates no significant impact on scope of gases considered pyrophoric and does not expect wholesale reclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemically unstable gas definition and sub-classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt Rev. 7 definition: 'a flammable gas that is able to react explosively even in the absence of air or oxygen.' Under Table B.2.1, a Category 1A chemically unstable gas is further subclassified: Category 1A/A chemically unstable gases are 'flammable gases which are chemically unstable at 20°C (68°F) and a standard pressure of 101.3 kPa (14.7 psi)'; Category 1A/B chemically unstable gases are 'flammable gases which are chemically unstable at a temperature greater than 20°C (68°F) and/or a pressure greater than 101.3 kPa (14.7 psi).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers should apply these temperature/pressure criteria to determine appropriate subcategory of chemically unstable gases and communicate hazards accordingly in Appendix B.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes under Table B.2.1 for flammable gases (default and thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rev. 7 added clarifying notes: Note 2: 'In the absence of data allowing classification into Category 1B, a flammable gas that meets the criteria for Category 1A shall be classified by default in Category 1A.' Note 3: 'Spontaneous ignition for pyrophoric gases is not always immediate, and there may be a delay.' Note 4: 'In the absence of data on its pyrophoricity, a flammable gas mixture should be classified as a pyrophoric gas if it contains more than 1% (by volume) of pyrophoric component(s).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply default-to-1A in absence of data for 1B; recognize potential delayed ignition when assessing pyrophoricity; when pyrophoricity data are absent, classify mixtures as pyrophoric if >1% by volume pyrophoric component(s) (subject to comments suggesting stricter thresholds/testing requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance and test-method paragraphs for pyrophoricity and chemical stability (B.2.3.x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed B.2.3.1 updates referenced consensus standards and testing methods. Proposed B.2.3.2 included guidance on test methods to determine pyrophoricity. Proposed B.2.3.3 provided guidance regarding when testing should be considered for pyrophoric gases and how to classify flammable gas mixtures if testing has not been done. Proposed B.2.3.4 provided guidance on test methods to determine chemical stability, including references to the most up-to-date editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposed to incorporate by reference updated ISO/IEC/other standards (e.g., ISO 10156:2017, ISO 817:2014, IEC 60079-20-1, DIN 51794, UN Manual Part III) and to change 'should' to 'shall' to make certain guidance mandatory, add U.S. units, and clarify when testing is required or discretionary. OSHA did not propose to require reclassification of previously-classified chemicals solely due to new methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder concerns and potential stricter practices (Cal/OSHA comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cal/OSHA suggested more conservative approaches: revise Note 3 to emphasize testing and factors influencing ignition delay; delete B.2.3.3 because it gives producers discretion; and change Note 4 from 1% to 0.01% and 'should' to 'must' requiring testing for any flammable gas containing ≥0.01% pyrophoric component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comments reflect an alternative, stricter risk-averse interpretation (err on the side of classification and testing). OSHA considered but did not adopt these stricter changes in this final rule; classifiers should be aware of such stakeholder positions and the potential for future regulatory updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not change regulatory definitions out-of-scope without notice/comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments about changing the definition of 'article' vs 'item' (as used in DOT vs HCS) were considered out of scope because OSHA did not propose updates to the definition; similarly, comments proposing wholesale adoption of Rev. 9 for explosives chapter were considered out of scope for this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA will consider clarifications in guidance documents but did not change regulatory definitions not proposed; labelers/classifiers should follow the regulatory text as finalized and watch for future guidance or rulemakings for clarifications or broader adoptions.
